Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here’s how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of “up to” 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state’s housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California’s checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it’s doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that’s only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge “unusually large” architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay “substantially above-market” wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward “pilot” programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn’t gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home’s purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today’s rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It’s not solving the affordability crisis.
It’s just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.

DIVISION 3. OBLIGATIONS [1427 - 3273.91]

PART 4. OBLIGATIONS ARISING FROM PARTICULAR TRANSACTIONS [1738 - 3273.91]

TITLE 14. LIEN [2872 - 3081]

CHAPTER 2. Mortgage [2920 - 2968]
( Chapter 2 enacted 1872. )
ARTICLE 1. Mortgages in General [2920 - 2944.10]
( Article 1 enacted 1872. )
2924.13.
(a) As used in this section:
(1) “Borrower” has the same meaning as defined in Section 2929.5.
(2) “Mortgage servicer” includes the current mortgage servicer and any prior mortgage servicers.
(3) “Subordinate mortgage” means a security instrument in residential real property, including a deed of trust and any security instrument that functions in the form of a mortgage, that was, at the time it was recorded, subordinate to another security interest encumbering the same residential real property.
(b) The following conduct constitutes an unlawful practice
in connection with a subordinate mortgage:
(1) The mortgage servicer did not provide the borrower with any written communication regarding the loan secured by the mortgage for at least three years.
(2) The mortgage servicer failed to provide a transfer of loan servicing notice to the borrower when required to provide that notice by law, including, but not limited to, the federal Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act, as amended (12 U.S.C. Sec. 2601 et seq.), and investor or guarantor requirements.
(3) The mortgage servicer failed to provide a transfer of loan ownership notice to the borrower when required to provide that notice by law, including, but not limited to, the federal Truth in Lending Act, as amended (15 U.S.C. 1601, et seq.), and investor or guarantor requirements.
(4) The mortgage servicer conducted or threatened to conduct a foreclosure sale after providing a form to the borrower indicating that the debt had been written off or discharged, including, but not limited to, an Internal Revenue Service Form 1099.
(5) The mortgage servicer conducted or threatened to conduct a foreclosure sale after the applicable statute of limitations expired.
(6) The mortgage servicer failed to provide a periodic account statement to the borrower when required to provide that statement by law, including, but not limited to, the federal Truth in Lending Act, as amended (15 U.S.C. 1601, et seq.), and investor or guarantor requirements.
(c) A mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent shall not conduct or
threaten to conduct a nonjudicial foreclosure until the mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent does both of the following:
(1) Simultaneously with the recording of a notice of default, records or causes to be recorded, in the office of the county recorder of the county that the encumbered property is located, a certification under penalty of perjury that either:
(A) The mortgage servicer did not engage in an unlawful practice as described in subdivision (b).
(B) The mortgage servicer lists all instances when it committed an unlawful practice as described in subdivision (b).
(2) Simultaneously with the service of a recorded notice of default, sends both of the following documents to the borrower by United States certified
mail with return receipt requested to the last known mailing address of the borrower:
(A) A notice providing that if the borrower believes the mortgage servicer engaged in an unlawful practice described in subdivision (b) or misrepresented its compliance history, the borrower may petition the court for relief before the foreclosure sale.
(B) A copy of the certification recorded pursuant to paragraph (1).
(d) Upon a borrower’s petition to the court for relief before the foreclosure sale, the court shall enjoin a proposed foreclosure sale pursuant to a power of sale in a subordinate mortgage until a final determination on the petition has been made.
(e) It shall be an affirmative defense in a judicial foreclosure proceeding if the court finds the mortgage
servicer engaged in any of the unlawful practices specified in subdivision (b).
(f) The court may provide equitable remedies that the court deems appropriate, depending on the extent and severity of the mortgage servicer’s violations. The equitable remedies may include, but are not limited to, striking all or a portion of the arrears claim, barring foreclosure, or permitting foreclosure subject to future compliance and corrected arrearage claim.
(g) A borrower may also petition the court to set a nonjudicial foreclosure sale aside when a certification required by subdivision (c) was never recorded or when a certification recorded pursuant to subdivision (c) indicates that the mortgage servicer engaged in an unlawful practice described in subdivision (b) or misrepresented its compliance history.
(h) Any failure to
comply with the provisions of this section shall not affect the validity of a trustee’s sale or a sale in favor of a bona fide purchaser.
(Added by Stats. 2025, Ch. 22, Sec. 2. (AB 130) Effective June 30, 2025.)

content.thinking:
I'm looking at Civil Code 2924.13, a provision AB 130 added in 2025 to shield borrowers on subordinate mortgages from improper servicer conduct, such as foreclosing after the statute of limitations has run. Prop 37's section 51515.04(g) exempts Prop 37 loans from that section, which seems to be a deliberate consumer-protection carve-out for the program's second mortgages.

I'm checking how the 2924.13 protections apply to these second mortgages, and I see the text lets borrowers ask a court to block foreclosure sales on subordinate mortgages after servicer misconduct like late statements or foreclosing past the statute of limitations. Prop 37 exempts its loans from that, so I'm noting it as a detail an opponent could raise. Next I'm turning to how HJTA has positioned itself on the measure.

I'm checking how the Heritage-style voting guide lines up with the Capital Lincoln Club page, which seems older. The HJTA guide explicitly urges a No vote on 37, so I'm treating HJTA as opposed. Supporters so far are SD Taxpayers and Berkeley Political Review, while the Mercury News rejects both 1 and 37 on demand-side grounds about mortgage costs and prices. I'm going to read the rest of the Mercury News endorsement for its points on builders and construction defects.

I'm going to pull the rest of the Mercury News endorsement, since its argument about builders and construction defects is the piece I still need. I also want the Yes campaign's own analysis, to check the 190,000 figure they're claiming.

I'm now checking the labor requirements the measure would impose on builders, since that's the part I still need to pin down. The text ties builders to labor and enforcement provisions from a specific subdivision of the Public Resources Code, with some conditions depending on project size and craft requirements.

I'm checking what Labor Code 218.8 requires, since the measure extends its obligations to developers, and I'm also looking at whether California YIMBY has taken a formal position on Prop 37.

I'm weighing the case for Prop 37 on its merits: no direct state cost since the bonds are repaid by borrowers, and a real focus on the down-payment barrier that keeps many would-be buyers out. I'll also need to check the strength of the demand claims against the polling I've seen.

I'm weighing the endorsements and the design features next: the consumer protections like the fixed rate, fee cap, and audits, plus the supply-side builder option aimed at condo defect liability. I'm also noting the broad coalition of supporters, from newspapers and labor to realtors and the governor, as I consider whether this is a better path than the alternatives.

I'm now weighing the case against the measure: the monthly payments on a second mortgage add cost, the rate isn't fixed, and the below-market pricing depends on philanthropic purchases that aren't guaranteed. I'm also considering the risk that subsidizing buyers in a supply-constrained market could push new-home prices up, a concern raised by the Mercury News, the OC Register, and the Union-Tribune.

I'm weighing the drawbacks now: the high income cap, which reaches well past first-time or lower-income buyers, and the critiques from the LWV and Hoover. I'm also considering whether restricting eligibility to new construction could push buyers toward distant, wildfire-prone areas with high HOA and Mello-Roos costs, and whether the "no taxpayer risk" claim holds given the pressure a state backstop could create.

I'm weighing the drawbacks of the measure's structure: the terms like the rate would be set later by CalHFA, so voters can't know the final cost. The text does cap the rate and fees, but the actual interest rate remains unknown, and the LWV and Mercury News both press on that uncertainty. I also want to check whether the HJTA's debt objection holds up given that these are revenue bonds.

I'm weighing the balance now: the measure looks like a modest, low-risk-to-taxpayers experiment with real but limited upside, while the bigger concerns sit with borrowers and possible price effects. I'm still uneasy about the unknown interest rate, the doubtful supply gains, the 200% AMI cap, and the builder liability changes, and I still need to settle on a yes or no answer.

I'm weighing whether a typical buyer comes out ahead: the program could let middle-income households buy new homes without any direct taxpayer exposure, but the cost is a second mortgage at a rate that isn't set yet, probably somewhere around 6-8%. I'm comparing that against the usual routes, like PMI on a low-down-payment loan or saving toward 20% down, to see whether the second lien is actually a better deal for someone who couldn't otherwise buy.

I'm weighing whether the monthly second-mortgage payment, which lenders would count against the buyer's debt-to-income ratio, could rule them out, so the program helps mainly middle-income buyers with income but little cash. I'm also starting to consider whether the demand-side price concern from the Mercury News and others is big enough to outweigh that.

I'm checking the PPIC estimate that the program could reach roughly 113,000 buyers in 2024 if every loan went to a maximum-priced home, which suggests the $25 billion pool may be too small to move prices much unless it's used broadly. I'm still weighing how that reach compares with the new-home supply response, which is uncertain given California's land-use and cost constraints.

I'm estimating how many new homes California sells in a year, roughly 60,000 to 80,000 single-family plus a smaller number of condos, to see how big a share of buyers this program could reach. If many of those buyers used the 17% second loan, it could add enough demand to push new-home prices up, though the 3% down, income, and debt-to-income limits would hold uptake down.

I'm wondering whether California's new-home sales are big enough that the program could meaningfully move prices, since if it finances a large share of those purchases the effect could be significant. I'll need to check that rather than assume it, since I'd be inferring it, not relying on a source.

I'm going through the other voices on the measure now: the editorial boards and groups backing it, like the Chronicle and the Terner Center, and those opposing it, including the Register, the U-T, and the LWV. I'm also noting the public poll, where about 65% said yes, and that the core question is whether a demand-side second mortgage helps buyers without enough that it hurts prices.

I'm weighing whether this design, limited to new construction and paired with builder liability relief, is a net positive for middle-income buyers, since down payment assistance usually nudges prices up when supply is tight. The measure tries to offset that with its new-build restriction, which makes the supply-friendly case worth taking seriously. It's a close call that depends on how much weight I give to affordability versus price risk.

I'm weighing whether to answer with a bare yes or no, given the user's constraint, versus adding a brief reason so the answer doesn't mislead on such a complex measure. I'm leaning toward leading with the yes-or-no and keeping any justification to a sentence or two.

I'm still weighing whether to give a bare yes or no, since the user asked for only that, against adding a short reason so a complex measure doesn't get a misleading one-word verdict. Leaning toward leading with the answer and keeping any justification to a few brief points.

I'm going to check the Mercury News editorial's full argument about builders benefiting from the program before settling on the answer.

I'm going to look for research on whether down payment assistance programs actually push home prices up, since that's the crux of whether this design helps buyers or just raises what they pay.

I'm going to check whether the AEI analysis of the Harris down payment assistance proposal actually found a price increase, and what size it estimated.

I'm checking whether the academic work on condo liability laws actually shows defect liability is a major driver of the decline, since that determines how much the builder-liability relief in this measure would matter for supply. I'll also look at whether the Realtors' funding of the measure raises a conflict worth weighing, and how long implementation would take.

I'm noting that the measure's rates and terms would be set later by CalHFA, and that the Legislature could amend it by a 60% vote, which gives room to fix problems but also means it could be weakened. I'm also looking at the consumer protections, including cash-flow underwriting for applicants with thin credit. Next I want to check whether there are any pending legal challenges to Prop 37, particularly over the ballot label or voter guide arguments.

I'm looking at whether Dream for All's quick sellout shows strong demand for down payment help, though that program had no monthly payments, which Prop 37's second loan does. So the demand signal may not transfer directly to this design.

I'm planning to check the rest of the Mercury News editorial, look at a condo liability study and an AEI analysis of down payment assistance price effects, and see whether there's any litigation over the Prop 37 ballot label.

The home price cannot exceed 125% of the county-level conforming loan limit under the Federal Housing Finance Agency standards.

Proposition 37: No Recommendation
September 23, 2026
Max Dubler

by Max Dubler
Introduction
Providing down payment subsidies for first-time homebuyers is a good idea on the merits, but is problematic in a severely supply-constrained market like California.
Prop 37 authorizes the state to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a second mortgage program to help qualifying homeowners afford a down payment on a new home.
It also establishes a new construction defect paradigm for homes purchased with Prop 37 loans.
Analysis
How Would the Down Payment Assistance Work?
The bonds would support a $25 billion fund that will offer second mortgages that cover up to 17% of a home’s purchase price (to qualify for a mortgage, homebuyers often have to provide a 20% down payment to get the best rate). The downpayment assistance would be paid back as part of the homeowner’s mortgage payment.
Prospective homeowners who use the fund will have to have lived in California for at least a year, make under 200% of area median income, provide a down payment of at least 3% of the purchase price, and move into the new home as their primary residence within 60 days of closing. The home price cannot exceed 125% of the county-level conforming loan limit under the Federal Housing Finance Agency standards.
The interest rate for these second mortgages will be dependent on the interest rates for the bonds that finance them, which means they may be higher than typical mortgage rates. While the program can deliver some modest savings to homebuyers by allowing a smaller downpayment without private mortgage insurance, larger savings would be heavily dependent on the ability to sell the secondary mortgage bonds at discounted rates.
Prospective buyers will be required to retain a licensed California real estate agent or broker “to ensure that the homebuyer receives adequate representation and consumer protection throughout the homebuying process.”
What Does California YIMBY Think Of This?
California YIMBY’s mission is to make California an affordable place to live, work, and raise a family. We advocate for supply-side solutions to the housing affordability crisis because housing prices are set by supply and demand; so building new homes at scale is the only way to address the housing shortage that is driving up prices.
Historically, homebuyer subsidy programs like downpayment assistance have exclusively worked on the demand side, often worsening overall affordability (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/how-will-first-time-homebuyer-assistance-affect-the-housing-markets/) by injecting more money into already-competitive markets with a limited number of homes.
Proposition 37 is different in that it can only be used for new homes, including single family detached, townhomes, condos, manufactured homes, or newly-converted, adaptive reuse projects. In theory, this means it would drive housing demand specifically toward new construction, which aligns with our goals of expanding the housing supply.
Would it work? One possible mechanism is that Prop 37 would make prospective homebuilders more confident in finding buyers, and thus more willing to build. We view this mechanism as quite unlikely. There is no shortage of buyers for newly built ownership housing in California (in fact, bidding wars are quite common).
Another possible mechanism is that Prop 37 would, like other downpayment assistance, drive up prices, but only for newly built housing. This would then induce homebuilders to invest in building more housing. Supply effects would be strongest in places where homebuilding is currently marginal: “second tier” neighborhoods/cities and exurban areas where demand is not as strong.
It’s worth thinking through the winners and losers of that scenario. Buyers using the program would benefit by being able to buy a larger, better located, or nicer home than they could otherwise afford. Buyers of new housing not using Prop 37 would lose out, paying higher prices. Indirect benefits would flow to some mix of buyers for older housing (who might face less competition bidding up the price) and renters (who might see more available rental stock to the extent Prop 37 moves people from renting to homeownership). Savings for homebuyers using Prop 37 would be muted by the associated price increase.
How well that price increase translates into new homebuilding depends on the price elasticity of housing. Such an estimate is beyond our scope, but we can look to what happened when home prices spiked from 2020-2022 in California as a reference. There is a downward blip in 2020 (the pandemic) and an upward one in 2021 (most likely shifting of permits from 2020), but overall the numbers are flat, consistent with our belief that constraints other than demand are the most important limit on development of new ownership housing.

How efficient a program for homeownership would this be? Proponents have estimated that it will build 190,000 new homes (if buyers are found for all the bonds, which is not guaranteed). That would place the bond revenue per new home at approximately $130,000 (not counting interest on the bonds!), repaid over the 30 year span of a mortgage. This estimate, however, assumes that 100% of homes purchased through the program would not otherwise be built. For the reasons discussed above, we find this assumption unlikely, and the bond cost per newly built home is likely to be higher than the average secondary mortgage. To be fair, that bond cost is not public money, but it still represents a substantial commitment of state administrative capacity.
What else could the state do to advance homeownership with the administrative capacity and potential resources (proponents have argued they will sell bonds at reduced rates to foundations and other philanthropic buyers) of this bond? Programs to bring down construction finance costs for builders, such as a revolving loan fund or loan credit enhancement reserve, would likely be much more effective. Like the secondary mortgage, they would only need to cover a share (10-20%) of total cost. But because construction loans have much shorter terms than mortgages, such programs could recycle the initial investment 6-10 times in the period a mortgage turns over once. And by directly reducing the cost to build new housing through lower cost financing, such programs would likely be much more efficient at converting their subsidies into a net increase in homebuilding.
Most of the legislation California YIMBY has sponsored in the past has been oriented around making it easier to build “infill” housing in existing neighborhoods, rather than the new single-family subdivisions on undeveloped “greenfield” that is often referred to as sprawl. Given the current regulatory constraints on new home deposits; on building new condos; and the resulting shortage of new infill housing for ownership, it’s likely that this program will primarily benefit people buying new homes in greenfield subdivisions until the legislature addresses constraints on new infill ownership housing.
While we understand that many of our grassroots YIMBYs are committed urbanists with strong commitments to environmentalism, and a dislike of sprawl, some greenfield is going to be part of ending the housing shortage.
That said, due to the ongoing housing shortage and continued constraints on home building, this program will probably not make homeownership more affordable, except in fairly limited cases. New homes tend to be more expensive than older homes. While downpayment assistance might help families with solid incomes and limited savings to buy homes more quickly, their monthly payment will be substantially higher to cover the 17% down payment assistance. Buyers will also have to pay a fee to the licensed real estate agent or broker that the law requires them to retain, increasing prices by 2-3%.
Recommendation: Neutral.
If we are going to subsidize demand for homes, this is one of the better ways to do it. However, given the ongoing shortage, such subsidies are unlikely to reduce costs for prospective homeowners.
